options.D: Attention runs over the whole vocabulary, and each token's attention share is its probability

prompt: Which backend pattern is the residual stream most like?

options.B: A cache in front of a database: each layer checks the stream before recomputing a value
options.C: A load balancer that routes each word's vector to whichever layer is least busy
options.D: An append-only log, or a request context that each middleware enriches rather than replaces

prompt: Which backend pattern is the KV cache most like?

options.B: A write-ahead log used for crash recovery
options.C: Sharding: each layer's keys and values live on a different machine
options.D: Memoization: compute once, store, reuse because the inputs can't change

prompt: What does continuous batching change?

options.B: The batch size is fixed at server start and every slot is kept busy by queuing requests

options.D: Prefill and decode run on separate models, so new prompts no longer pause the decode loop

Why use top-p instead of sampling from the full distribution?

options.A: It guarantees the same output every time, because the cut removes all randomness from sampling
options.B: It makes generation faster, since softmax only has to run over the few tokens that survive the cut
options.C: It cuts the long tail, so one unlucky draw can't derail a long answer, yet keeps variety among plausible tokens
options.D: It shrinks the KV cache, since tokens cut from the tail never need their keys and values stored on the GPU

prompt: Why is prefill compute-bound while single-user decode is memory-bound?

options.A: Decode does more math per token than prefill, because each output token must attend to the whole prompt again
options.B: Prefill reuses each weight it reads across every prompt token; decode reads all weights for one token per user
options.C: Prefill runs on the CPU while decode runs on the GPU, whose memory is slower to reach than the CPU's
options.D: Prefill skips attention and only runs the MLPs, so it has less memory to read per token than decode

Why stack 32 blocks instead of one very wide block?

options.A: All 32 blocks share one set of weights, so depth adds reasoning steps without adding any parameters
options.B: Depth chains steps: a later block uses an earlier block's note (“it's a riverside”) to add one (“floods likely”)
options.C: Each block handles a different slice of the vocabulary, so 32 blocks cover more tokens than one wide block could
options.D: Stacking shrinks the KV cache, because only the last block keeps keys and values for earlier tokens

prompt: What exactly does the KV cache store?

options.B: A copy of the model's weights in faster on-chip memory
options.C: Every earlier token's key and value vectors, for every layer
options.D: The query vectors of every earlier token, in every layer

prompt: With a KV cache, what does each decode step compute?

options.A: q, k and v for every token so far, then attend over all of them as on the first pass
options.B: k and v for every token again, but q only for the new token, then attend over the fresh k and v
options.C: Only the logits for the new token, since attention was already done for the cached tokens
options.D: q, k and v for the new token only; append its k and v to the cache; attend over the whole cache
